utterances.text: Now you said all your orders were issued to you by your battalion commander. When he issued you orders did he ever tell you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Object to -- mischaracterizes what paragraph 35 says, says all my orders from my battalion commander, not all my orders were delivered by my battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, I will read it back again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do it again, yes please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, you say, "All my orders from my battalion commander Colonel Budimir were delivered verbally." Now, when Colonel Budimir issued you verbal orders did he tell you pursuant to whose order, that is, did he tell you I received these orders from such-and-such of my superior commander and now I'm issuing you this order pursuant to his order -- that person's order. Did he inform you pursuant to whose orders he was issuing you orders?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He didn't tell me whether it was pursuant to orders from the chief of the administration or from General Gotovina. And I never asked him to give me that information, nor did I consider it necessary, if my battalion commander was issuing me with a certain task.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And did you ever see any written orders issued by Mr. Gotovina to Mr. Budimir?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, I know in court we saw a lot of documents, a lot of orders issued by General Lausic. Did you see any written orders during that time issued by General Lausic to Colonel Budimir?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in the course of this trial or do you mean in the course of my work in the town of Knin?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In the course of your work in the town of Knin.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not see a single order issued by General Gotovina, or, rather, General Lausic to the battalion commander while I was in the town of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, did you ever refuse an order or an invitation or a -- a request, so that we cover all those words, from Mr. Cermak to you?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please clarify your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, during the course of Operation Storm and in its aftermath, actually in its aftermath when you were in Knin, did you ever --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm objecting to this question because it is far too general. I think we need to be specific. Which invitation are we talking about. We can't just talk in generalities. Mr. Kay covered all of this ground yesterday. Let's be specific, a specific invitation for a specific task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, I had the same question on my mind. Therefore, I will put it to the witness. He apparently did not understand the question. Yesterday a lot of questions were put to you about how you considered your position in relation to Mr. Cermak. Some orders were shown to you, signed by Mr. Cermak, and you finally explained that, in light of paragraph 37 of your 2004 statement, that you felt that were not under a duty to obey any orders. You considered them to be invitations. You corrected your statement, where it said he invited me to go there, so you -- you gave quite some details on that matter. Now, was there ever, and could you identify, ever any invitation or order, or whatever you considered it, that you deliberately have decided not to follow. So could you identify from any of your meetings with Mr. Cermak, do you remember any instance where you thought he asks or requests or orders or suggests that I would do so-and-so, but I will not do it for this and this reason. Could you identify any such instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, to the best of my recollection, there was a task from General Cermak where it was suggested to me that security should be set up for a protected facility. I can't be sure anymore what the name of the facility was. I know, as far as I can remember, that at the time, I told General Cermak that I could not carry out this task because I did not have the men available who were needed to carry out that task, and I suggested that, if possible, this should be delegated to the civilian police, for them to do it on their own. How many other similar instances there were, I can't tell you right now, but I do know that such things did occur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you -- you said you do not remember the facility.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a civilian building. It might have been a factory, a post office, or something similar, but I can't remember precisely what building it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that you found yourself in an impossibility to do what he asked you to do? Is that how I have to understand your answer? And that you then told him that this was the situation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you said there were "such things did occur." Could you be more precise. How many other similar instances there were you couldn't tell me but you know that they did occur.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember, Your Honour. This is one instance that came to my memory when you put the question to me as to whether there were any situations where General Cermak asked me to do something and I didn't carry it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just for the record the incident that he just referred to is also included in paragraph 47 of the 2004 statement P875.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: One last question, Mr. Dzolic. Now, we had some evidence about what tasks were carried out at check-points yesterday and even today. Mr. Misetic showed you some documents. Yesterday Mr. Kay showed you your daily orders where you sent off military police patrols and set up check-points or sent people -- shifts for check-points. What was the main -- what were the principle tasks of the military police patrols, what were they supposed to do, patrolling the area?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To best of my recollection, the tasks of the patrols in the town of Knin were the following: Visiting the check-points to check whether everything was in good order; monitoring the situation in the town; and in accordance with their powers, taking action in relation to perpetrators of breaches of discipline or criminal offences. Also, military police patrols could be sent by the duty officer in the company to a certain location if the duty officer had information that something was happening at that location.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And can you also tell us what the tasks of the check-points were?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And that would be my last question.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, the tasks of the men in my company at the barrier check-points were those stemming from the rules of work of the military police. That is, to monitor entry and exit into and from the town of Knin. In other words, to control the traffic. And to take action in accordance with their powers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you be a little bit more specific about the last sentence: "To take action in accordance with their powers." What were their powers and what were the actions they could take?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If, at the barrier check-point, they stopped a motor vehicle and established that the vehicle was being used to transport things and equipment which could be assumed to have been stolen, that person was to be detained at the barrier check-point until the arrival of a military police patrol, which would then take over the suspect, and, if a warrant had been issued for the arrest of a person or for a certain piece of equipment, if this was found at the check-point, they were authorised and had the task of confiscating the vehicle or confiscating the piece of equipment or the object that was being sought. I hope that clarifies that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It does, Mr. Dzolic. Thank you very much for answering my questions. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise for going beyond the time I estimated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Gwaunza has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dzolic. If you could refer back to your statement of 2004, paragraph 9. It is recorded there that, and it is attributed to you that: "If the military policeman saw a crime being committed by a civilian, then he was obliged to contact the civilian police and hand the civilian over to the civilian police." My question is: Would you know what happened in the case where a civilian police or civilian police witnessed or saw soldiers committing crimes, what would happen in such a situation?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, and also the way I understand the status of an authorised official and the powers and tasks of such an official, a civilian policeman should act in a similar manner. That is to say bring into custody that person or rather to the station, then the military police would be informed, and then the perpetrator of the said crime would be taken to the military, if it is a member of the Croatian military, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Thank you. I have another question for you, and this pertains to paragraph 23 of the same statement. Sorry, it's paragraph 24 of the same statement. You mention there that: "The reason for us guarding the cemetery was to protect those who were bearing bodies." I want to ask, why was it necessary to guard those who were bearing the bodies?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've already answered a similar question put by the Prosecutor. However, I believe that I need to repeat that to you as well. What happened was a particular situation, namely when we received information to the effect that an unknown person had fired at or towards soldiers who were carrying out exhumation at that cemetery. For that reason it was decided to put a security detail there, so that the people involved could continue doing their job unhindered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And the last question I have pertains to your 2008 statement, paragraph 22. And there you were clarifying what you had said in paragraph 61 of your 2004 statement. You talk about in the middle of that paragraph : "After stopping the vehicles, the brigade commander's authority was given retrospectively to alloy those guards to be transported." I think this was in reference to what happened at check-points. I want to know whether you recall any instance in which such authority was denied, the brigade commander's authority, and what would happen then.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in that case, the same kind of action would have been taken as I have already explained when I spoke of what official persons did at barrier check-points. The said person would be kept there, a patrol would be called in, and then the said person and the vehicle would be taken to the military police unit. The equipment would be confiscated. The person would be handed over to the crime police, and further action would be taken in accordance with legal procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Sorry. I said that was my last question, but I have another question and that will be my last question. The following paragraph, the same statement of 2008, paragraph 23, towards the end, you mentioned there or in the middle of the paragraph: "Depending on the seriousness of the crime and the value of the property stolen, the perpetrator could be sent to the military prosecutor or the matter was treated as a misdemeanour." I want to know whether you know what would be regarded as a misdemeanour.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as I can remember, a misdemeanour was a situation in which the benefit in terms of property did not go beyond a certain level that was defined by law. As far as I know from that time, well, I don't know whether this is the actual amount of money involved but it was up to 1.000 kuna. That was supposed to be -- considered to be a misdemeanour. Beyond and above that, it was a crime and there was criminal responsibility involved. It is this that sense that I spoke when I said that there was a difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one additional question in that respect. At that time how much Deutschemarks would a thousand kuna be?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, right now, I really cannot say whether it was 150 or whatever. I don't know exactly. I really do not remember how much it was at the time, the value of that money, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Kinis has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Referring back to your statement 2004, paragraph 61, 62 and 63, and Judge Gwaunza also touched up on this issue but I would like to ask this question a little bit in different style. How do you know about such orders that brigadier commanders can authorise for persons to do some illegal acts regarding property and you should justify this? Did you have some written instructions or how do you know this?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that by making my statement to the Prosecution, I did touch upon this, because I said that there were one or two cases when we stopped a column of the Croatian military when there was a change of shifts on the ground. We noticed certain objects that could lead one to believe that it had been stolen, that they had been stolen, rather. Then I contacted my superiors because the persons in those vehicles, that is what the commander of this column claimed, namely that they had been allowed to take this with them. Then I sought guidelines in terms of what should be done with regard to this matter. What I was told was that if the brigade commander states in writing that that was now army property and that it would be used for meeting the needs of the army, then such a column should be allowed to pass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Which superior directly issues this order for you?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- well, I don't remember whether I asked for approval or guidelines from Budimir or Juric. I don't know if they contacted the commander of the said unit and whether they decided or defined that. At this point in time, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: And then is next my question: In the first annex which are also on the roads, [indiscernible] the rules governing the structure and operation of the military police was then in force in the Republic of Croatia, and in particular referring on paragraph -- Article 10. You are policeman, a person who has some kind of legal knowledge. I don't know whether you know or what is a public law and what a private law, but my question is what do you understand that the term security in public law and order should be task of military police, whether it could include also such situations that you are -- can obey a law, simply?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I should obey the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: You should obey the law. Could you please tell me were such directions from your superior should be recognised as a law at that time or police should follow to -- by law.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police was supposed to comply with the existing law. However, by your leave, Your Honour, may I explain what this was all about, in this particular case, when these approvals were given. I, and my superiors probably, believed that if the brigade commander had signed an approval to let such equipment pass, then possibly this equipment had been exempted from military facilities that were in the town of Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: But could you please tell me or maybe you name a title of law on which you based your activity in such style. I cannot recall every country where commander order can replace a law, and you are a policeman. You know very well what is the law and what is just order.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do understand what the difference is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking you questions.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Could you please name title of law under which you operate at that time.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you the exact name of that law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the name. I don't know what I would call it, was it the Law on Criminal Procedure, was it the penal code?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: And penal code or law replace articles which are included in penal law by others of army commanders.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not saying that they were suspended by an order issued by my commander. In this case, I'm not saying that there were any violations of the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: I cannot understand. Was there violations or not or there wasn't violations of law under your understanding at that time.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time in such situations, to my understanding there were no violations of the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you as well. You just explained, answering a question by Judge Gwaunza, that you secured the cemetery on the 6th of August, because soldiers who were carrying out exhumations were shot at. Is that -- it may be there that an a translation issue, but that's how I understood it. That's how it appears on my transcript.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not say that the military police were securing soldiers at that point in time. These were members of the civilian protection who were in charge of burying dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So they were active in burying bodies and they were shot at. How did you -- was it a patrol you sent there or was it expected and did you have a -- a small team there? Because I do understand that you secured that cemetery during more than one day. You said "until it was taken over by the civilian police."

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that I said that the civilian police had taken over that particular job. For how many days we provided security, I cannot say with any certainty. I think it was a day, or two, or three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what caused, exactly was it reported to you, someone is shooting at those who are burying people at the cemetery, or ...

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were these officials who were carrying out this job. They provided this information to us that they had been shot at and it's on the basis of that information that we took these security measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have a clear recollection that that happened on the morning of the 6th or the afternoon or the evening?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't remember exactly when this was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you -- did you include this securing the cemetery in your daily orders on -- well, let's say the 7th and the 8th or the 9th?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember that. However, it is possible that this should have been recorded in written form in the daily order. If not, then probably a particular person would be appointed who would be made available for that particular day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you send one person, did you send more persons?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly whether it was one or two persons, but it certainly wasn't more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you check in your daily orders whether this task appears for those days? That's D787. Mr. Registrar, perhaps we could ask the witness to look at page 4 out of 79 and following in the original. Or to have -- I don't know there's a possibility otherwise to have it printed out for him.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot see it there now. What I can see here are barrier check-points. If it can be scrolled down a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and perhaps for the other days to see whether it appears in this ... Perhaps the next four or five pages and then ask the witness to ...

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing's moved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. You'll be provided with a ... Could you try to find this task in the ...

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't see the task for the 6th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you see it for the 7th or the 8th? Mr. Registrar, 7 and 8 would go up to and include the tenth out of 79 pages.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot see it here. Namely, that the task had been spelled out precisely for that day. Or, rather, for securing the cemetery. It is not stated very specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I take you to paragraph 32 of your 2004 statement. Yes. Would you please read it. Numbers are appearing in this paragraph. First, it says that -- that additional military police arrived and you give a number of 70 to 80 people. And then a bit further down it says: "That gave us about 140 to 150 mainly experienced military policemen in total in Knin." Were these 140 to 150 all under your command or is this the joint company with a total strength of 140 or 150, or do I misinterpret your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, including the forces with which I entered Knin and then the additional forces that came in, all of that made up that joined or combined company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that was -- they were there on the 6th or -- and the days following until you left on the 12th. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. They stayed behind, after me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, if I look at the daily order, I find tasks assigned to a number of persons by far smaller than 140 to 150. For example, for the 9th of August, I find tasks assigned to, at least by persons named, 61, in total. You may not have the 9th, but I counted the small lists. If you want to look at the 9th, then, please, it could be put on the screen.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can put it there, but I think there is no difference between that and the orders that were on the previous days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that's numbers not amounting to 140 to 150 but rather 70 or 80 or 60.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as I can see here, the Drnis barrier check-point involves a total of 12, three shifts of four men respectively. Then 34, 46, 48.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're looking at the 9th? What date are you looking at?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking at the 7th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not the same for all days, I do agree with you. I didn't look at the 7th primarily. If you say it amounts up to 140, 150, then ... It may be that I have difficulties in finding my way through the original and you're looking at the 7th. I was looking at the 9th, as a matter of fact, but you might not have that in front of you. You may understand, were all the tasks included in this -- in these lists or were there tasks assigned to persons which do not appear in these lists?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, those people who were not engaged in writing over here, they were supposed to be available. They were resting. So it is from that shift that these persons would be engaged, if necessary, for similar tasks, like the one that we mentioned, providing security for the cemetery or, say, a task involving going to collect the mail, carry something, whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were they having rest or were they on various duties? I do not -- is it your testimony that you said, Some of my men did not have just a daily rest but they were not on the schedule for that day at all. They had a day off?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My statement is that those persons who were not on the list here, in terms of being engaged but who were available nevertheless there in the unit, then these persons were engaged or, rather, could be engaged for other tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would that mean that this daily order does not cover the complete activities of the joint company?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim that with certainty. They should be here on this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me move to another subject, Mr. Dzolic. Briefly, I think your testimony was that you took civilians to the school in Knin in order to protect them.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you said how should I call them criminals. That is at least what is my recollection of what the threat may have been to these persons. What criminals did you have in mind? What -- what did you want to protect them against, what information you had about criminals going around and threatening civilians?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not have any information. Rather, I had an order stating that these people should be taken to the collection centre. Probably Commander Lausic, when providing such guidelines, had had experience from previous actions. I'm primarily referring to Operation Flash. For the sake of prevention, that is, so that something similar would not happen. These people were taken care off in collection centres. They were not taken away only to be taken care of but also in order to be registered as being there, and, as far as can I remember, in order to have official IDs of the Republic of Croatia issued to them, personal IDs, things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now I hear a lot of explanations. Were they taken there to protect them against criminals on the basis of earlier experience; or were they taken there for documents to be issued to them. You said, Maybe the order I received was based on ... do you know what it was based on exactly, or is it just that you are guessing or speculating?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not know on the basis of what the order was issued. I -- well, probably it seems that I was speculating, when I say that I assumed that that could have been the basis for that kind of an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now were you aware of issuing documents to those persons in the school, was it organised there? Did you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have any knowledge in order to be able to make any assertions. It is just that I remember, on the basis of memory, that it was said that such documents would be issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, could I -- and that might be the last subject I will cover. Some questions were put to you in relation to your statement, your 2004 statement in relation to war booty. In paragraph 61, you're talking about military taking electrical property like stoves, televisions refrigerators in trucks through a check-point. In paragraph 63 of your statement, you're talking about war booty being property belonging to the enemy army, which, as you stated -- now, I'm seeking clarification of what you observed and what your view on transporting such goods were. Did you consider televisions, stoves, refrigerators to be goods that could be legally transported and pass through check-points?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not consider this to be equipment that could legally be taken across check-points or through check-points but if there were one or two TV sets, that did not lead me to think that it could have been stolen from civilian properties. These TV sets could have been at military installations. It is from that aspect that I was assessing the situation. If that is what it was, then it could have been the military property of the enemy army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you ever further check or investigate whether these televisions came from army facilities?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember that this kind of an investigation was carried out. Because if the commander had signed that this equipment was military property, I thought that this was a regular thing. I've already stated earlier on that if the commander would notice that a soldier of his is committing a disciplinary infraction then he was supposed to take certain steps in according with the rules on military discipline. If the commander guarantees by way of his own signature that it is a regular thing, then I believed that there were no elements there involving the commission of a crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, at the end of paragraph 61, you say: "As a policeman, I did not agree with this." And you were talking about that authorities was signed -- was obtained and that these goods were let through. You said: "As a policeman I did not agree with this, although it was better for the property to be removed than burned or destroyed, which was happening." I'm trying to reconcile your testimony until now, and I see the following, that on the one hand you say well, these television sets could been, well, say, military television sets. I take it then that the same is true for the refrigerators and the stoves. Why did you then not agree because they could be seized they would fall within the -- within your definition of war booty, that is, property belonging to the enemy, which was legally, rightly taken over by the Croatian forces. Would did you then not agree and why did you say that it was better to be removed than to be burned or destroyed, which seems to be inconsistent with your definition of war booty and how to handle property taken from military facilities.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, to the best of my recollection, when I uttered this sentence saying that I disagreed with this, I think I was referring to the investigator's question as to whether I agreed in general to the theft of property in such a way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You considered it to be theft. What you were talking about in --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I considered it to be theft if people were taking away equipment belonging to civilians. In this case, I did not have any awareness or information that these things were being taken out of civilian buildings. Rather, I considered that the property was being taken from military facilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then again why did you disagree that a signed authority was obtained? I mean that is exactly what you would expect if these were military goods. It comes as a surprise did you not say this is exactly what should have been done because it was my definition war booty, and therefore I did fully agree with that to happen and comes as a surprise that you apparently look at it as something illegal.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree that if the equipment was taken from military facilities, it was regular; but when the investigators were putting questions to me to which I was responding, saying that I don't agree, I don't know whether they were asking me whether I disagreed with the taking out of military equipment from facilities, military property, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Yes, I have to look at the clock. Before we -- will there be any need to put further questions to the witness, Ms. Mahindaratne, on the basis of the issues raised by the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Just one question, Mr. President, from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And for Mr. Misetic, how much --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have several questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Several questions. Then I think it would be better to allow -- to give Judge Kinis an opportunity to put the one question he has on his mind, then have a break and then ... Judge Kinis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Thank you. One small question. Yesterday during cross-examination Defence counsel Mr. Kay presented -- submitted as evidence two orders issued by General Cermak. On one of them was provide inspections under all UNCRO convoys, including helicopters. My question is simple: Did you obey this order? This is the first question, and the second, if yes, what specific tasks you carried out for the purposes.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not know whether there was any talk of inspection or of providing security. As regards military helicopters. We neither could nor did carry out inspection of UNCRO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't have D number at my disposal right now but I would look at this -- there was something --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Judge Kinis, I can assist you on that, it is P512.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we put on screen, please. As you can see the first point first is: UNCRO helicopters must be inspected before each flight. The inspection should be carried out by military police. That's what my question is.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we carried out no inspection of UNCRO men. We only provided security when they were taking off and landing. I don't remember that we acted pursuant to this order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: It means that you didn't obey this order?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could say that. I don't remember that this order was ever implemented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question in relation to this before we have a break. Would that mean that you said we -- you provided security taking off when helicopters would take off. Was there a special team assigned to that or was it -- would you receive a call one helicopter is now taking off or will take off in ten minutes? How did it -- how was this organised?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't remember, but most probably a flight would be announced and then either a patrol would be sent or an officer -- a police officer would be designated to carry out this task of providing security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a break. We will resume at ten minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber understands that the name of the cells, being holding cells, has taken a rather literal meaning at this moment as far as Mr. Markac is concerned, because they can't open the door anymore, from what I understand. So that then really becomes a holding cell. Mr. Cayley, we understood that there was no objection against proceeding and we hope to see Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, we already discuss it. No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then an opportunity will be put to the parties to put further questions to the witness, although the Chamber has mainly -- has not raised any new issues so, therefore, the parties are not invited to start full new series of questions. Only matters that were triggered for the Defence of course in your re-examination and for all the parties during the questions put by the Bench. Perhaps it is most practical, Ms. Mahindaratne, if I give you an opportunity first so that the Defence can then cover everything what is included in your questions and then we'll conclude. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, in response to a question from the Bench with regard to measures taken to protect civilians, I'm referring to that situation where you were required to take civilians to the Knin school, you responded in this manner. You speculated, actually, and you said, you speculated: "Probably commander Lausic in issuing guidelines may have used it -- issued such guidelines based on his previous experience and previous action." And then you went on to say I primarily refer to Flash. Now, did you have any information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, in one of the follow-up answers, as you already explained, the witness said that it was speculation, should we now investigate that background of what appears to be speculation rather than anything else?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I was simply -- on the speculation part of it, I was just on a follow-up question and perhaps if is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: But I ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- now to explore Flash where the witness says that whether it was inspired by the experience in Flash is purely speculation that would start -- the Chamber is not encouraging you in exploring Flash in any further detail at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. Then I will not ask any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: First as a housekeeping matter, I'm advised, Mr. Dzolic, that in an answer you gave to me earlier when I asked you who was present at the meeting in the video that I showed you, the translation came back as a minister of the Croatian council, and let me just ask you if what you intended to say was the minister of the Croatian Defence Council or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, these are not questions which arise from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do agree, Ms. Mahindaratne, that they do not arise, so therefore, Mr. Misetic, if you would have followed my instructions very precisely you would have asked permission for that, but it is so obvious that if something is on our transcript not in the right way, then of course it doesn't -- it is just seeking to avoid errors and mistakes which can be avoided but I formally do agree with you that Mr. Misetic should have asked and if I would have been in his position, I might not have done it either because it is so obvious that no one could possibly could complain about it. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you Your Honour, and I apologise, Your Honour, I just didn't want to -- wanted to make sure it wasn't the Croatian minster of defence but rather from the other side of the border. But since it is clear ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, in response -- or to follow up from some questions from the Bench, in this case, we have evidence that in the town of Knin, the ARSK had three military barracks, the northern barracks, the Senjak barracks, the southern barracks, two schools that were used to garrison soldiers of the ARSK, a police station, the ARSK headquarters, the location of an intelligence service of the Republika Srpska Krajina and that the old hospital in Knin was used to house officers of the ARSK. My question to you is: At a check-point, after Operation Storm, how do you as a military policeman determine whether a TV set, a refrigerator, a bed, a stove, was taken from one of the facilities that I've just identified or was taken from a private apartment? How do you make that distinction when you're standing at a check-point?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can't tell that. We can't distinguish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That the only thing you can do is rely on a certification by a commander of a unit as to where the goods were taken from in order for you to then let them pass through a check-point?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's correct. That's what I attempted to tell the Chamber through my explanation. But I don't know whether I was sufficiently clear. I seem not to have been very clear. It was not my wish nor is it my wish to confuse Their Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I understand that. When we were talking with regard to certain portions of your statements, sir, when you called up the commander of the unit that was at the check-point, was it so that you could obtain from him information as to where these goods had come from, whether they had come from one of the facilities I had just read out to you or whether they had come from a private residence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, do we have a basis -- are we talking about 61?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Basis for what, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A basis for the factual ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We don't have a basis for the other factual in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. It only says in both cases assigned authority was obtained and they were allowed through. The role of the witness in this respect is factual role he played or whether he tells what -- what was reported to him by his men is not clear to me. If we are talking about 61.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We are talking about 61, Your Honour, as well as paragraph 22 of his 2008 statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Which was a clarification of 61 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- that wasn't read out to him where he says in 61, paragraph 61 from 2004 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- I gave the impression that truckloads of personal electrical goods were being transported by military trucks. What I wanted to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- was in a couple of instances, in a military convoy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Still -- still ... one second, please. I'm mainly referring to line -- page 73, line 3. And I will check it again. When you called up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I could be wrong. I understood his answer to -- in response to one of the questions from the Bench that he contacted the commander of the unit. I could be wrong, but that's what I thought he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was the only issue, yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Would you like me to check on it before I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may do so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you contact the commander of the unit to obtain his permission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we first ask whether he was present at the check-point. That's the issue which is -- was bothering me primarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Were you at this check-point?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So how did you come to find out what transpired at the check-point?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The men who were at the check-point informed me of the situation happening at the barrier check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And did they tell that you they contacted the commander of the unit?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't tell me that they had contacted the commander of the unit, but they contacted me and I contacted my superiors. They, in turn, contacted the commander of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So in these conversations with your superiors -- between your superiors and the commander of that unit, you don't know how it was determined whether those goods had come from one of the military facilities in Knin or not, do you?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 22 of your 2008 statement you clarify and say that this only happened in a couple of instances. How much is a couple of instances? Let's be specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I object to that, Mr. President. He doesn't say that this happened in a couple of instances. What he says, what I want to say was that in a couple of instances in a military convoy. He is describing the event in relation to a couple of instances, not that it happened in only a couple of instances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Rephrase the question that takes the least time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did it only happen in a couple of instances? Is that what you meant to say, sir?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, what does it mean "a couple of instances," how many?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Two, okay. Do you recall which brigade it was?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We've heard some testimony in this case about TVs. How -- being at a check-point, again I have to put it to you, how do you know where the TV came from?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where that TV came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You say -- I believe you've testified that you were -- let me -- strike that. Confiscated goods from check-points were ultimately relocated into the Senjak barracks. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that the Senjak barracks was the logistics barracks of the ARSK before Croatian army took it over?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall, but there were depots in that barracks with military equipment and food, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could go back, Mr. Registrar, to D734, please. If we can go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is from the 11th of August. Again, this is the report of Major Juric to General Lausic. And again at paragraph numbered 4 on the 11th of August, Major Juric says: "In the crime military police section perpetrators of crimes (misappropriation of property from the liberated areas) are being processed daily." Now, we've talked now about these two incidents of a convoy being allowed to pass. Was it also your experience that at these check-points people in fact were being detained and then processed by the crime police section for misappropriation of property?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, I showed you earlier this morning and if necessary I can show it again, Mr. Juric reporting about an Ursus, U-r-s-u-s, tractor seized from Lieutenant Grgic, a Labin Progres milling machine seized from Private Marko Gutic. If these items were in fact being seized, would that indicate to you that military personnel were in fact having property seized from them at check-points?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't respond to that, because Colonel Jenjic had his own area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction captain, Captain Jenjic.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I don't know how this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Turning to the issue of civilians in Knin, were you going -- was the military police in Knin forcing civilians out of their homes and taking them to the school?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this -- to what extent is this triggered by?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: A series of questions on civilians being taken to the school, why they were being taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But not whether they were taken by force or not. Just the witness has given an answer under why and I think the why was explored, not the methods by which.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The matters by which may be relevant to the why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then you could have asked about it. Of course everything triggers a new element. You can make a chain with that, but the only thing I explored is the source of knowledge of what the witness said about it. That's the only thing I explored, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I mean he is the military police in Knin so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not saying-- but I'm not saying that the witness might not have knowledge about it, but at this stage in the examination of the witness more is required than just that the witness has knowledge about a certain matter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Going back to the issue of the check-points, this is my last question, when you allow -- you. When the military police allowed the convoy to pass after an authorisation had been received from the military commander, was it your understanding therefore that the commander was certifying that these goods were not -- had not been seized from private property?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my understanding, yes. That would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is that why you told the Trial Chamber that you did not believe that a crime had been committed in the first place?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any of the other Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Nothing arises. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, Mr. Markac, it's good to see that your holding cell has not held you for the remainder of the day. It was an unfortunate matter that you could not leave your holding cell. The Chamber is glad to see you back. Then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the Bench has no further questions to you either, Mr. Dzolic, this concludes your testimony. I'd like to thank you for having come to The Hague and having answered the questions put to you by the parties and by the Bench and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have booked sessions for this afternoon. It might not be a good idea to start now for seven minutes with the next witness. There are two options, I would say. The first one is that we would continue until 2.00 and then start later, not at 2.30 but -- for example, but that not be a good idea because then the lunch break would be too late. So I suggest that we take an early break now, that we resume in 52 minutes that's at 2.30. Mr. Hedaraly, you needed one hour from what I was -- more or less?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. I am quite confident that I can complete the examination in less time, maybe 30 to 40 minutes. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then the estimates of the parties are such that we could conclude this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe that absent some things that come up, I think that I will be doing most of the cross. I don't think my learned friends have much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would mean that we'll still try to finish in the second afternoon session. We will have a break, and we resume at 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.40 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Registrar, we are still in a follow-up session, which means that there's no need to call the case, which was done during our first session this morning. Mr. Hedaraly, are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We are, Mr. President, thank you. The Prosecution would like to call Mr. Lennart Leschly to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher. From what you just said, no application for protective measures. Did I understand well that meanwhile all the parties have made their submissions on the 92 ter application and that there are no objections against either the statement, dated the 6th of February, nor against any of the attachments?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Leschly. Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration, the text of which will now be handed out to you by Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Leschly. Mr. Leschly, English is not your mother tongue, or is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not. If you have any difficulties in understanding questions or in expressing yourself, please let me know. You're first examined by Mr. Hedaraly, who's counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Hedaraly, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Leschly. Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Lennart Leschly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: I am retired, having been in the Danish Army with a gap of 22 years where I was not serving in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And when did you retire?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: I retired in 2003, when Danes turned 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could have 65 ter number 5433 on the screen, and if I could have Madam Usher provide a copy of the -- hard copy of the statement and the reports prepared by the witness. First of all, could you confirm that the document that is on the screen in front of you is the same that you have in tab 1 of the documents that were just given to you?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Do you recall providing a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on 6 February 2008?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And is that statement in front of you the statement that you gave on 6 February?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it should be 6 February 2007.

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: My apologies. And did you have a chance to review the statement yesterday?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Does this statement accurately reflect what you said to the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor in the course of the 6 February 2007 interview?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And are the contents of the statement true to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Finally, if you were asked the same questions today in court that you were asked on 6 February 2007, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: That, I thoroughly assume, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would like to have 65 ter 5433 admitted into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there are no objections, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P888.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P888 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I would also tender at this stage the six weekly reports prepared by Mr. Leschly, covering the events of August and September 1995 that are referred to in his statement. I can take them one at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so so that we have them all on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: The first one is a weekly report dated 13th of August, 1995. That is 65 ter 4074.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel is kindly asked to slow down and to make pauses between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next one would be, Mr. Hedaraly?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: The next one will be 65 ter 4110, the weekly report dated 20 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the next one would be ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: 65 ter 4155, weekly report dated 27 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: After that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: 65 ter 4248, weekly report dated 17 September 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: 65 ter 2124, weekly report dated 24 September 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the last one?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: 65 ter 4269, the weekly report dated 1 October 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, numbers in this sequence to be assigned to these documents would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, these would be Exhibit number P889 up to and including P894.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P889 up to and including P894 are admitted into evidence. You may proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to read out a short summary of the evidence of the witness contained in his statement to inform the public of the contents of the witness statement that has just been admitted into evidence. "Lennart Leschly was a field monitor for the European Community Monitoring Mission (ECMM) in Knin, Split and Zadar from September 1993 until April 1994. From October 1994 until January 1995, he worked in the Information Section of the Croatia desk before becoming UN liaison officer for the ECMM in February 1995. "On 6 July 1995, he was appointed head of the ECM Regional Centre in Zagreb. Mr. Leschly received various situation reports from the various ECMM teams, including the team that was based in Knin after Operation Storm. "Based on the information contained in these reports, he produced weekly summaries of the political, humanitarian, military, economic and infrastructural situation in Croatia which were forwarded to the ECMM headquarters in Zagreb, and from there to the various European capitals. As the head of the Regional ECMM Centre in Zagreb, he met with a number of civilian and military leaders in the Krajina, including General Ante Gotovina, who he met in Knin in September 1995." This concludes my summary, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Leschly, can you please briefly explain to the Court the reporting structure within ECMM, sort of the teams, the CC, the RCs and the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes. The starting point of reporting comes from the teams. The teams are in the field. They conduct meetings and they report on their findings, both facts and impressions. They send their report to a coordination centre, so-called CC, that will typically have two, three, four teams attached to it. The CC then will make their report and send it on to the Regional Centre that will gather the information both from the CC reports and the team reports. These reports all go to the information section in the headquarters. That's where I was at the Croatia desk, and there was of course a Bosnia desk next to us. And here all the reporting is gathered and used for the daily report which was sent out to the foreign offices of the EU countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And can you tell us, the teams that were reporting in the former Sector South, which CC or RC did they come under?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: All right. Well, we have to -- we have to distinct between before late August 1995 and after. Before late August 1995, the Regional Centre in Sector South was in Knin, and it was a regional centre reporting directly to headquarters. And it was -- in that respect, it was a colleague to Regional Centre Zagreb. So Regional Centre Knin did not report to me until around 1st of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said that the teams reported directly to the Regional Centre in Knin, but earlier you said that the teams would report to a coordination centre. So was that an exception?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: There was an exception. In Sector South, inside the RSK, there were only three teams, and they would report directly to RC Knin, mainly because of the geography. It was more practical. They were co-located. On the other side of the frontline at that time, there were teams in Split, in Zadar and in Gospic, and these three teams reported to the Coordination Centre Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you mentioned there was a distinction before late August and after late August, so what was the reporting situation after that change was made?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: When Regional Centre Knin was closed down, there were some times -- I mean, today I can't quite remember in which order they happened during these, well, couple of weeks. At a certain time, RC Knin, still calling themselves "RC Knin," apparently showed up in Zadar, but eventually it became a CC in Split reporting to Regional Centre in Zagreb. There was no point in having a regional centre in an RSK that no longer existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And that CC in Split therefore reported to you?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Registrar, if we could have Exhibit P889 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And that is, Mr. Leschly, your weekly report of 13 August 1995, which is the second tab in the package in front of you, and it's going to come up on the screen for everyone else to see. And I want to ask you about the summary of that -- of that report, in the top half, and it says: "The Croatian execution of Operation Storm delivered to Croatia exactly what the country wanted; land without people. It revealed HV as equal to any other Balkan army when it comes to unnecessary looting and brutality, and it created the largest single voluntary ethnic cleansing during the entire Balkan conflict." I'll just pause for the translation. My first question for you, Mr. Leschly, is: What did you mean by "voluntary," when you mentioned it in that summary?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: I have to admit when I look at it now, it's perhaps not the best-chosen word. "Voluntary," at that time, I'm quite sure I meant "without putting up a real fight." One could then argue that "voluntary" means that it is something you do even if nobody had asked you to do it, and I'm quite sure that the civilian population there did not want to leave, so the "voluntary" is, you're right, it's not a very good word, but it was an ethnic cleansing without any major fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So when you're talking about "without putting up a real fight," are you talking about the army of the former RSK?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just object to leading. If he wants to ask him what he means, that's fine, but I don't want him putting words in the witness's mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm just trying to clarify the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The problem is that if there's no fight, it's difficult to define between whom there was no fight. But you could ask the witness who was involved in these events. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Leschly, who didn't put up a real fight?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: It was the army of the RSK. We had expected perhaps some more fighting, because at some time earlier, I can't remember whether it was July or June, there had been a parade in Sector North which apparently was showing, from what one of our monitors had reported, a renewed military strength inside the RSK, so on the basis of that observation it was very noticeable how little resistance took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, isn't it true that there was a basis for this question in the written statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The answer to -- the question should be, "What do you mean," don't say -- you know, give him the lead of exactly what Mr. Hedaraly wants to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But isn't the lead not yet in the written statement which is in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It depends exactly what angle of that version. I take it it's not just a written statement that we're discussing, but the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, but of course, if a clue to an answer of the next question has been given already by the witness, then of course it's rather a follow-up than leading the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But if we go back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. If we go back to the actual question, the line, if we could put it down "without putting up a fight," that's not in the statement, if you look in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed and not spend more time on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we go to the bottom of the page in this report, the last four or five lines, and I'll read it to make sure I don't mischaracterize anything and draw an objection, it says: "At the time when it had become quite apparent that the methods of the HV was as deplorable as those of the" and that's "Bosnian Serb Army," "BSA, the US, with immaculate timing released pictures of freshly disturbed earth in the Srebrenica area, pushing the Croatian stories down the list of news worth covering." Now, my question for you, Mr. Leschly, is: Are you equating what happened in Srebrenica to what happened in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: No. It's not nearly -- no, no, no, but there was at the time, if I recall it correctly -- we are, as we all know, these 13 years back. An interesting difference between the press coverage internationally of atrocities made by one side and atrocities made by the other. But you're absolutely right. Srebrenica, as we know today, is in a different league from what happened in RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And what was so interesting about the difference between the press coverage?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: I'm -- now we get to the memory. I'll be 65 on Monday, so -- but I remember one CNN bit where they claimed that some European observers, which of course was us, had noticed something, and then after that it was immediately turned down. That was in the Croatian area. And then came a very, very thorough, for good reasons, coverage of Srebrenica, but it was a noticeable sort of putting these two things up next to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we just go to the third page of your report, that third full paragraph, the first one under the heading "Humanitarian Situation," there is a figure there of 200.000 Krajina Serbs that you say had left. Now, just to be clear, does that figure reflect both Sector North and Sector South?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes, it does. From the best of my knowledge, I remember when I arrived in 1993, the figures -- the figure that was normally mentioned for the population of Krajina was 400.000, and then apparently quite a lot had left during that period, so that the number in August 1995 was then down to 200.000; not that any one of us were able to count it, but that was the figure normally referred.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Is if we can now go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, I'd like to ask the witness: You said the figure that was normally mentioned for the population of Krajina was 400.000 and then it went down to 200.000. Were you referring to the whole of the population or were you referring to the Krajina Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Krajina Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can go to P890, and that is your 20 August weekly report in tab 3 of the package that you have. It's going to come up on the screen soon, and I want to ask you about the first page, the second paragraph, under "The Political Scene," the first two sentences: "All through the Balkan conflicts, the creation of a Greater Serbia has been heralded by Croats and Muslims as the ultimate evil. Now there seems to be just as much relevance in talking about a Greater Croatia."

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Court what you meant by "Greater Croatia"?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Well, the word "Greater" here again perhaps is not the right one, but Croatia within the geographical borders of the geographical Croatia, which of course hadn't been the case as long as Krajina existed. So it was -- it was the Croatia proper, really, could be a better word.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And what about the composition of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: The composition, I'm not quite sure I understand the word. What is put together of --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I meant the ethnic composition of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Well, it was my impression all through -- as I mentioned also earlier, that Croatia was not keen on having a Serb minority inside its border.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And did that impression -- was that impression related to you using the term "Greater Croatia"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I just ask for facts. I mean impressions, et cetera, is not facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You could ask for the source on which he based this impression. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Court, what was the basis for this impression, to the extent it was reported in your -- in this weekly report?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Right now, when I search my memory, I wouldn't be able to do that. No, I don't know. Not a specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To the extent non-specific?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, in a mission like that, you know, you talk and you meet people, and you discuss, and probably it came up at a certain time. I can't even remember who it should be with. But the two words -- yeah, the two words look similar, so Greater A, Greater B, and I think it -- now I'm really digging deep. It was something like what did not -- what Milosevic did not manage to do, Tudjman seemed to be able to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although there may be some confusion, Mr. Hedaraly. I think you were asking about on what Mr. Leschly's impression was based that Croatia was not keen on having a Serb minority inside its border. Could you tell us on what you based that impression, whether with specific or less specific sources?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would say all through -- all through my duties as a monitor, also in the first one which was in Sector South and in Split and Zadar, it was quite obvious that, on the one hand, the Serbs did not want to be part of Croatia and, on the other hand, the Croatians were not keen on having the Serbs inside their border. That was -- that was a general trend all through all the meetings that we had with a lot of people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're more or less confirming and, to some extent, repeating your impression. The question was specifically about your last answer. You said something about meetings. Meetings with whom; what was said at these meetings? Either you have a specific recollection on what was said on a certain meeting or you have a general recollection of the kind of things said by ambassadors, by Croatian authorities, by Bosnian authorities. I'm just -- that's what Mr. Hedaraly is seeking and what might assist the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, and I can just say that I -- I can't recollect that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
