utterances.text: I want to move on to a meeting that is ascribed in your statement that you had with Mr. Gotovina. Can you, first of all, describe for the Court what were the circumstances of that meeting, how it got organised and so on?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Are we talking --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm talking about a meeting in September.

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: In September. Where are we? We are --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm just asking generally, from your recollection, what were the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Okay, yeah. When Regional Centre Knin was closed down and Regional Centre Zagreb took over that area of responsibility, then it was a very natural thing that I, as head of that regional centre, toured the area now under my area of responsibility, and met with the important people in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court who you met with as part of this trip?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: I met with the chief of police in Gospic, Zupan in Zadar, the -- what was it. You're much better remembering names than I am. The -- Norac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I want to help the witness. It's reflected in P893, which is the witness's report of the 24th of September, 1995; 65 ter 2124, tab 5 in your book.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I wanted to ask the witness, without first referring to his report, what his recollection was, but it's fine for that -- for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Court -- you referred to the Zupan of Zadar in Zadar. Can you tell the Court what that is, what the position is?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Zupan is the head of a "zupanje," which I think the best English word is "county."

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, going to the meeting itself that you had with Mr. Gotovina, what was the -- what was the atmosphere in the meeting? Was it a formal meeting, was it informal?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: It was -- well, I think all of the meetings that we had with people, they were always quite friendly and always, you know, a bit relaxed, but then naturally, during these meetings once you get to perhaps some of the more difficult points, then you may have periods where the temperature cools down. But otherwise I think we tend to always act in a polite way. We were a diplomatic mission, and therefore we never wanted to create anything other than a good atmosphere between the people with whom we meet or met.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And throughout this series of meetings that you had in those days with the various responsible people there, what was the -- what was the main purpose -- or what was your main purpose in talking to them?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: The purpose, of course, was to find out the new situation and find out how they looked at it so that, and again back to our main mission was to make sure that the European governments were as well informed and briefed on matters in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And what were the topics that you would generally bring up at those meetings?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Well, what is the situation, any news, "What do you think of ... " if there were any specific encounters. There might have been -- I can't remember specifically here. Now I'm talking on how did we conduct our meetings and what did they expect from the future. Was there any new developments that, you might even say, they would like Europe to know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And referring specifically to your meeting with Mr. Gotovina, how did that meeting start? What was the first -- what was the questions or -- if you remember?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: No, I mean, probably said, "Hello." I can't recollect any specific opening remarks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we go to your report that has been pointed out to you by Mr. Kehoe, at P893, the second page, the bottom paragraph, you state in your report: "When Lieutenant General Gotovina, commander of the Split Military District was asked if he shared the Zadar Zupan's opinion about the need for a state of emergency in order to have avoided the killings, lootings and burnings, his only remark was, 'What killings,' after which he went into an attack." Let me just stop here.

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yeah, this --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me just ask you, first of all, my first question. Do you remember that portion of the conversation taking place?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Reading what I wrote some time right after the meeting means, of course, I have a recollection of what basically took place, but if you ask me about specific sentences and statements, I have to pass. But there was no question about it that when it was mentioned about why do these things take place, I must have thought at the time that General Gotovina did not recognise killings or lootings or burnings. I think that what -- "killings" covers these activities overall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I just want to make sure that it's not a translation issue or a language. When you say --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, excuse me. If we want to talk about a specific translation, we're speaking English here. I don't believe that there is any translation issue between two English speakers, so I would object to going back into this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, Mr. Hedaraly said, "It's not a translation issue or language." I take it that translation must have been a slip of the tongue, because there is no translation. If there's a language issue, Mr. Hedaraly, you can raise the matter in several ways; either by putting the question again, where you may have some doubt as to whether it was fully understood. If you want to discuss or raise what the language issue is, then we would have to ask the witness to leave the courtroom so that the witness will not be influenced by your remarks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will note that the witness did not raise a language issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly did, and please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: First of all, I want to clarify something that he says, and this is my examination, so I'm entitled to clarify something that the witness has said if I don't think it's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I allowed you to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: What did you mean by -- I'll have to scroll back up now. Just a second. What did you mean by, "General Gotovina did not recognise killings or lootings or burnings"?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: That when it was mentioned, he certainly did not say, "Yes, we have been conducting lootings and burnings and killings." He rather said, "What," as if it was something that was nonexistent. And when I look at it today, what I'm saying is that if he had said, "What killings," that doesn't mean that he has admitted lootings and burnings. I think that covers general atrocities, if that's a better word.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Then in your report, you go on to discuss another portion of the meeting, where it says: "New nations are naturally very nationalistic in the early stages, and as he put it, once Sector East is home, he would possibly become more liberal, but not for now." What did you take that comment to mean?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Well, I -- I might have noticed this specifically, because I've had some experience with new nations and nation-building. I lived five years in Singapore in the early 1980s, and it was very -- very noticeable that they talked a lot about nation-building and what you need to do in the early stages of a nation. And I come from Denmark with a 1.000-year-old monarchy still the same family ruling, so to me that is something which I noticed, this thing about a new nation will do a lot to build a nation and make its mark. And once Sector East is home -- this is something I recall from that period in time, that a lot of talk always came up about now, now Sector West in May, Sector North and East -- and South in August. What about Sector East? And when we talk about Croatia proper, then of course, that should also include Sector East. And from what I read here, this is now -- you know, we've -- as if General Gotovina could have said that, "We are not quite there yet because there's still a sector that needs to be included, and then once it's included, maybe we didn't have to be so tough in our nation-building." That's the way I recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And what do you mean by "tough in our nation-building"?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Well, I've written the word "liberal," so probably I think it's something that we can't afford to be liberal in this early stage, but this is now -- we're not talking fact. We're talking impressions of some statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me just clarify. In your report, when you said that "once Sector East is home, he would possibly become more liberal," is that something that Mr. Gotovina said that you reported?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: I would expect so, since I wrote it down. But, I mean, we are 13 years back. I would think -- I would think so. And then as always with these meetings, you hope that the interpreters are good, because -- because that's where I get it. I don't get it directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And what did you take the word "liberal" to mean in this context?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Well, normally you would think easy-going, allowing some things that you otherwise wouldn't allow, words to that extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Do you remember who else was at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes. From ECMM, we had the deputy head of the CC, who was an Italian, and I can't remember his name. The other one was a monitor, and I can remember his name because he happened to be a Dane, Stig Marker-Hansen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can have 65 ter 3419 on the screen, please. You don't have a hard copy of that document. You'll have to look on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: This is -- can you first please confirm what that document is?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Counsel. I don't mean to interrupt. I do believe that there was a disclosure from the Prosecution without the redactions with regard to the authors here and 65 ter 3419.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That would have been an inadvertent disclosure. This is how we were allowed by ECMM to use these documents, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can you first of all tell the Court if you can recognise this document or if you can say what it is?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I saw it yesterday and I probably also saw it in 1995, but yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court what it is?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Well, this is a team report from a team by the name of "Kilo 1," and "Kilo" is Knin. And they send it to the CC, which at that time was Split, and they also send it in for the RC so that the RC has got it at the same time, and the other teams. And there you had the teams in Zadar, Gospic, Bihac, Karlovac and Velika Kladusa. UNMOs, UNHCR unit staff also get a report like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if we go to item 2, "Military Situation," it says "HRC, DHCC and TL K1 met General Gotovina." Can you explain who HRC, DHCC and TL K1 would be?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Well, I was HRC. DHCC was Deputy Head of Coordination Centre, Split, and I can't remember his name. He was Italian. I'm sure you might have it somewhere. And then you had the team leader of Team Kilo 1, and that was Stig Marker-Hansen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if you look at the second paragraph under that heading, it says: "Asked about the ongoing looting, arson and harassment, the general's opinion is that police has to control the situation and Croatia is still a nation with constitution, law and order. Any person committing crimes will be charged. However, a war is always followed by disasters and now things are under control." I'll just pause here for a second, and I want you to focus on this last part: "The general has no objection for Serbs to live in Croatia, but he regards as a human feeling to hate an enemy who has burned, looted and expelled one's family. The war will not be stopped by nice words of international organisations. Only a strong Croatian Army can do that." Now, is that consistent with your recollection of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes, it is, although we do not write in exactly the same way. It is very much the same. When I said something like "too early to become liberal," I think that is supported by "only a strong Croatian Army can do that." That means to be sure that things are under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Leschly. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just, counsel, if you will, I don't know if you're going to offer that document into evidence, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Yes, I would like to tender that document, 2D419.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which gives you an opportunity to tell me whether you object or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I was going to offer it myself if they didn't. I just assumed that counsel was going to. It was on the 65 ter list. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P895.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P895 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Leschly, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kehoe is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. You may proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Leschly. Mr. Leschly, I just would like to take you through a flow chart of -- excuse me -- of ECMM, and I'd ask you if you'd take a look at this and tell me if it's incorrect in any fashion. So if I could bring up 1D 530007. Now, Mr. Leschly, this is a flow chart that we have developed from the ECMM documents we've prepared, and of course this is before the reorganisation that you talked about on direct examination. And I'd just ask you to take a look at this. And frankly, Mr. Leschly, it appears to be correct, with the particular individuals involved.

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yeah, those -- those few, I actually remember the names, they are correct, and the others are not in my brain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But the head of the ECMM at the time was Mr. Sanchez Rau from Spain?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I guess maybe I'll ask this question in the back way. Do you see anything wrong with this particular document?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let me flip to the next page, and what I've done -- we have done - again this is prior to page 2 of this document, please - and this is again prior to the organisation, that we're just giving you a snapshot of RC Zagreb and RC Knin. Is that basically the structure that you had?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Leschly, as part of your duties, and you were the head of the Regional Centre Zagreb, but you were also head of the Danish delegation. I think they call it Dan-Del; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Well, not ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you were head of the Danish delegation?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Danish delegation, yes, head of the delegation, HOD, head of delegation. That was the normal abbreviation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I've just seen the variation called -- an acronym for the Danish delegation called Dan-Del, but maybe not. Okay. And the individual that I have in Topusko here is Mr. Ben Jensen. Do you recall him?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And he was part of the Danish delegation, and Topusko was in RSK area then, was it not?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I think the other individual, for instance, down in Knin, in Knin was Soren Liborius; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And they reported to Mr. Augarde?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you remember Mr. Augarde?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you confer with Mr. Augarde over the time when you were RC Zagreb and he was RC Knin?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes. As you can see from here, at this time we were two, well, colleagues. He had his regional centre and I had my regional centre, so at this time we were -- we were, both of us, reporting to headquarters. And later on, when Knin was closed down, then you have a different setup.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, did you confer with Mr. Augarde during your time when he was the HRC Knin and you were HRC Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: What do you mean by "confer"; that we would compare notes before report-writing, because in that respect I would say, no. We did our own reporting, and that would then meet in headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm talking more about just discussing matters with Mr. A ugarde.

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yeah, but we -- we didn't have that many meetings. We -- we took care of our own area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, under "U", the various coordination centres, and just looking at Mr. Jensen in Topusko, you relied heavily on those individuals who were in the coordination centres for the information you were receiving; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: That is correct, because these were our eyes out in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let me just go to the next chart, which is what I believe is the situation after the changes within ECMM. If we can go to the third page. Once again, Mr. Leschly, if you could take a look at this, and to the extent that you can advise us of anything that is incorrect in an y fashion to the best of your recollection.

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to say to the best of my recollection, I wouldn't be able to draw that myself now, but when I look at it, it doesn't look wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Based on that answer, Your Honour, we'll offer into evidence, 1D 530007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the fact that the witness can't see anything wrong with it after examining it for a few minutes, when he clearly does not recollect anything, does not authenticate this flow chart, so for that reason I'd be very cautious that it be admitted for the purpose that is there without the underlying material used for that. I mean, to the extent the witness can confirm some of the organisation, it's fine, but he's saying -- but then Mr. Kehoe changed his question, "Did you see anything wrong with it," and he looks at it for 30 seconds or a minute and says, "I'm not sure, I can't remember." I think we have to be careful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this about weight or admission?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It's about admission, the authentication of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When we're talking about documents, authentication is -- I think it's clear that it's a document created by the Defence, so I think that unless you would like to make any dispute about who made that document. But perhaps I have a wrong understanding of what "authenticity" means, bit I always understood that to be that can we -- is there any doubt as to where this document came from, who created it, et cetera? Is that the issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No, if that's Your Honour's view, then it's fine. Then it should go to weight, but it should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you have any other perception of what "authenticity" means, because I do understand that authenticity may be an admissibility issue, but then I want to understand what you actually said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Very simple. To the extent that it's about what the witness says about this document that gives this document its value, that's the concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness says that the Defence is not -- from his recollection, he has not seen anything wrong. I can imagine that you would not give much weight to that if there is no support elsewhere in the evidence for this, but then it's a matter of weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, frankly, the Defence jointly just wants to get this document correct. It comes from the documents that we received during the course of this, and if the OTP -- I -- even if they dispute any line in here, certainly we'll amend it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems to be a matter on which the parties could, if it's accurate, could easily agree without spending time on it in court, Mr. Hedaraly, because of course we --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It's the first time I see this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not blaming you for immediately saying, "I do agree," but these are typically matters on which I would expect the parties to see whether they could agree, rather than that we have to discuss on whether there were 30 seconds or 45 seconds available for the witness to look at it and to come to the conclusion that he has not discovered any inaccuracy in it. Please proceed. The matter going to weight. Mr. Registrar, the --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this becomes Exhibit number D797.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D797 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Leschly, I'd like to talk to you a bit about the reports that you have, and like the Prosecution, I'm interested in your first report of the 13th of September, where you talk, in the summary, about the situation involving Storm -- excuse me, the 13th of August, I apologise. You write the report for the period of time of 6 August to 12 August, and you're talking about the largest single voluntary ethnic cleansing during the entire Balkan war. And I'm interested, sir, in the word "voluntary." Now, if I may, sir, prior to this you were well aware of the situation in Western Slavonia in an operation that was known as Operation Flash; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: M'mm-hmm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I'd like to show you a document, and it is D60. This is a United Nations report dated 5 July 1995. And if I can go to the eighth page of that document, under the item "Refugees." Now, you recall, do you not, Mr. Leschly, that Operation Flash took place in May of 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: M'mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And let me just read this item for you from July of 1995: "During the first two days of military operation, as many as 10.000 people fled from the Serb-held area of Western Slavonia, mostly from the Okucani area, across the Sava River bridge into northern Bosnia and Herzegovina. The RSK authorities had previously held regular evacuation drills, and there are reports that some of the refugees may have been forced into leaving against their will." Now, tell me, before we move on to the next bit, about the regular evacuation drills that were being held in Western Slavonia. Do you know anything about that, sir?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You didn't learn anything about that during your time as --

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: It doesn't ring any bell to me today. I see this report, as far as I know, for the first time. There were quite a lot of reports, so I can only say that, yeah, that's taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Putting this report aside, if you will, do you recall learning at the time that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could I first ask: You're looking at a report. You say that's taken place. At the same time, you say, "I don't know anything about it, I haven't learned about it." Is it your testimony now that you say that this report says that this took place and that you take it for face value or do you have anything to add from what you learned from other sources? I would like to have your testimony clear on this issue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Inasmuch as I haven't seen this before and as much as I was not very much involved in that area at all, I do not have any substantial knowledge that can either turn it down or accept it. What I more or less said was, this is a report, yeah, well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say it's in the report, it's there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, yes. I don't have any -- any strong opinion on it, because I wasn't involved in this at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Putting the report aside for a moment, Mr. Leschly, did you ever learn anything about the fact that the RSK had been conducting regular evacuation drills in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: No, that's -- it's new to me. I mean, if I search --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just -- I think that question was answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was trying to put the report aside. I mean, I understand that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but then if you put a report which says there were evacuation drills, then you ask the witness, "Do you know anything about it," the witness says, "No," then I verify whether he has any knowledge, apart from looking at it, at that document, and I say, "Put the document aside. Do you know anything about evacuation drills?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You're right. I'm trying to clarify based on what is in the document, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... I just said --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Judge, but I'm trying to conduct this cross-examination to put it aside and to just ask him about whether or not he knows about the evacuation drills, report aside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Leschly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Repetitious questions, whether in chief or in cross, is similarly a bad use of our time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Leschly, were you aware of an initiative by the UN called "Operation Safe Passage," where the United Nations assisted Serbs from Western Slavonia to leave the area?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let me show you something. This is a video D136, and we're moving now into the Krajina in July of 1995. This is, in fact, a video from July of 1995, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Stop right at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, during the time, Mr. Leschly, when you were in RC Knin -- excuse me, Zagreb, and I will present to you that this has been offered into evidence as evacuation drills being conducted by the RSK, were you aware that the RSK was conducting evacuation drills prior to Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I mean, that -- he answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness has answered the question. It's for a fact. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Let us turn attention to D138.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is a report from 31 July 1995. If we can just blow that up. And I'm interested in -- this has to do with preparations for evacuation. If we can go to the middle of that page, starting with the word "Special," do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: "Special emphasis"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Special emphasis and the measures and actions that they are obliged to take in this regard. Special emphasis was put on sheltering and preparatory actions for an evacuation. The commission has completed their task reports from all local communes were submitted to the municipal Civilian Protection Staff today. Lists of people to evacuate have been updated. The fuel distributed in November 1994 has been checked, as has the roadworthiness of vehicles." Now, did the people that you had down in any of your regional centres in the Krajina tell you about, in their interfacing with the RSK administration, that these preparations, putting lists together, checking fuel, checking the worthiness of vehicles, that they were doing that in preparations for an evacuation, before Storm even occurred? Did they tell you that?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: The way I remember it today, no, I don't -- I don't recall that, as I think it -- it would have -- it would have not been consistent, I think, with the impressions that we got. But I wouldn't -- I mean, yes, there's bound to be some reports that I have missed 13 years ago, that today I wouldn't know. But it was not a major thing that was reported. I had another report -- you mentioned Ben Jensen, and he reported about a military parade which he very much thought showed that now the RSK, contrary to what at a certain time we thought, was able to put up some resistance. So -- and, again, as we have -- earlier today, I have explained the word "voluntary." That does -- I mean, this is a wrong word used, because it never, even in my mind, meant the civilian population voluntarily leaving, but it was -- there was no military real defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So is it your testimony, Mr. Leschly, that as you sit here now, you do not know anything about evacuation preparations that were made by the RSK prior to Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: I wouldn't rule out that it could have been mentioned somewhere, but it's -- it's -- if I had been asked to say were there evacuation exercises like that, I would probably say, "No," today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Turning your attention to the actual day of Operation Storm, and if we can just put on the screen D137, which is the evacuation order signed by Milan Martic at 1645 on the 4th. This was the evacuation order of 1645 on the 4th, where in item 1 President Martic talks about the planned evacuation; item 2, the evacuation to be carried out in a planned manner according to existing plan direction, are you familiar with that evacuation order?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is it a situation, Mr. Leschly, that you don't recall or your people in Knin did not inform you?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: I -- I don't recall having been informed about this. We know that the civilians, of course, left, and then as always when somebody goes on the move, they probably try to do it in as orderly a fashion as possible. But any specific paperwork behind that is something that I haven't come across.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My question to you, more specifically, is: Did the people in Knin tell you that the RSK authorities told the civilian population to evacuate according to the evacuation plan that they had established?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If he doesn't recall, how can he ask him if he was informed? He just said he doesn't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, Mr. Kehoe, it's now the second time that you ask this question, and we all saw the witness struggling to see whether there was anything on his mind that could assist him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'll move ahead, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then to ask a witness, "Were you not informed or do you have no recollection," of course is a question which --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- would never provide any additional information. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In Sector North, do you recall the RSK requesting the assistance of the UN to evacuate the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, I could to this from the bar table, Judge, rather than taking any time now. It's just a document that I will share with counsel, a UN document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you wrote this report back in -- and I'm talking about P889. When you wrote this report concerning the voluntary ethnic cleansing, you make no mention in the preface of this that this pertains to the voluntary ethnic cleansing, meaning the army, do you?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: I didn't quite get that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, when you say "voluntary ethnic cleansing," what you've told us today is -- and I turn to your statement that voluntary was -- and this is paragraph 14, "was the early withdrawal of the army." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: No. What I meant was that it really meant that there wasn't any now I say major fighting. I have to say that was probably more of the -- some of the more civilian in the ECMM. Quite a lot the others were serving officers. I wasn't. A bit too civilian there. But the fight that they might have put up, based on, for instance, this military parade that had been a month earlier, didn't happen, and that's why I write this. I may also cast a little light over the report I have seen, because one of the -- one of the interesting things about early August was that I was on leave when Operation Storm started, so reports coming on the 4th and the 5th of August would have arrived in Zagreb while I was in Denmark. It was something that some of them were not quite happy that I left, but I was necessary in Denmark; I wasn't necessary in Zagreb. I had a very able deputy, [indiscernible]. So there could have been some reports during those days where I was in Denmark, and then I came back. If I remember correctly, it was on the 9th or 10th, something like that, and so therefore this was sort of based on what I then picked up on when I came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Leschly, who was voluntarily ethnically cleansed?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Put that way, I would probably say nobody, because nobody wants to be ethnically cleansed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the question was which ethnicity, because when you're talking about ethnic cleansing, you're talking about an ethnicity which was cleansed? No, no, wait.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What word was that? Is that the ethnic background or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The ethnic background of those who apparently, you said, were voluntarily cleansed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this is what I have tried now -- we're at the fourth time to withdraw that word when it comes to the Serb population. I would like to withdraw that word, because I realise, of course, that it's not -- it's not a good word, and it should be reinterpreted into that there wasn't a major fight put up to avoid the leaving of -- and then the number of 200.000, I don't know, but that was a number we very often heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Leschly, in your statement, which is, if I may, P888, at paragraph 14, you say, in the last line, that the term "voluntary" was the early withdrawal of the ARSK. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. "Do you see that?" I want to make sure the witness has it in front of him, but it's not on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see that, but it's just been written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, we have it. Do you have your statement? If not, it could be provided to you so that you can read paragraph 14. Yes, that's your statement, apparently at least from what I can see at this distance. If you would just go to the page 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you find number 14?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 14, okay, yes. Yes, I want to say in relation to the military. It was certainly not the population that voluntarily -- but the military, that from where we looked at it in the international, they did not put up a very dedicated resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, as we can see --

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Somebody might disagree, but that was the way it looked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As we can see, there's no mention of that in your statement that you wrote at the time, and my question is: With regard to this "voluntarily ethnically cleansed," are you talking about the Serb civilians, the military, or both?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I would say the witness has now answered this five times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it has been addressed a couple of times. I'm just wondering what would be the best way. Mr. Leschly, apparently we all are trying to understand what you say in paragraph 14 to the best of our abilities. Now, there are several aspects in this statement, in this one. When you say they launched single voluntary ethnic cleansing, you said "I meant that in relation to the military." There seems to be two issues. First, ethnically cleansing on a voluntary basis apparently refers to people leaving an area. Now, when you were talking about ethnic cleansing, were you referring to the people as civilian population, or the military, or both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mainly, the civilian, and this is where the word "voluntary," I mean, it should be removed, because it's something which, in my mind, related to the military, which is the thing that I -- I never -- in comparison to a lot of my colleagues, I was very little into the military aspect of it, because I was civilian at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I thought I understood your explanation and the language you used in your statement to tell us and it has been dealt with today as well, that you use the word "voluntary," primarily, but -- correct me when I'm wrong, but primarily to express that the people leaving the area were not forced to leave by combat activity, and that to that extent it was voluntary, where you say it may not have been of their own free will to leave, because as you earlier told us, who would want to leave? Is that how I have to understand that basic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what you basically say in paragraph 14?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then if the parties would like to seek further positions, please. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So just to clarify this, the "voluntary" pertains to the army, and the "ethnic cleansing" pertains to the civilians?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes, that -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But the civilians didn't leave because anybody forced them to leave; they left when the army was leaving?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Because the situation forced it, you might say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let us continue on with your report, I mean, just staying with this 889. This comment that the -- in the second line: "The Croatian execution of Operation Storm delivered to Croatia exactly what the country wanted; a land without people." Now, the comment "land without people," now, did you get that comment from Mr. Jensen?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: It might be. I mean, I will not say "yes," but I will say that I would not rule that out, because that could have been -- the way I know him, it could have been something he could have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And do you know if Mr. Jensen got it from Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: I have no recollection of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you talked about this in paragraph 12 of your statement, if you can, you said that: "When I said that the country wanted land without people, it was based on what I had read, heard and later what I had experienced ..." Now, when you wrote this report on the 13th of August, 1995, you hadn't been to Sector South since Operation Storm, had you?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you wrote this -- if I read what you say correctly, this comment that you wrote on the 13th of August about Croatia wanting a land without people was written before you say you later experienced it; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: I don't quite understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Read your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I try to understand the question, is that Mr. Kehoe is asking you, but please correct me when I'm wrong, whether you wrote that and that the reference to the later experience, that you had not had that experience yet. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you wrote about -- now, it's perfectly unclear to me, Mr. Kehoe. Perhaps I leave it to you to put the question in such a way that the witness and, preferably, the Chamber as well understand the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to say that today I cannot recall my whereabouts in those days, but I wouldn't rule out -- I can't make it more precise than that -- that I had been down to Sector North when I returned from Denmark. I wouldn't rule that out, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The fact is that you wrote it, and you wrote in paragraph 12, you then -- that statement is based on what you experienced after you wrote it? Isn't that what you said in your report -- in your statement in paragraph 12?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Well, paragraph 12 here of course is -- that's something from February last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, sir. Read the first sentence to yourself.

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Oh, okay. It says later what I had experienced, so, yes, it is later. Further down in 12, there is another thing which is really -- again, like the "voluntary," I shouldn't have put it like that, "the actions on the ground as personally observed." I would say that what I personally observed was not action, because ECMM was normally kept away if there was any kind of military action. So that is -- that is a wrong expression to say "personally observe," because what I could personally observe was the evidence after things. We saw the slaughtered livestock. We saw burned houses and things like that. I was not near any kind of military action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you wrote here that it's based on what you have heard, the person you were hearing this from, in part, was Mr. Jensen?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Could be. I would not rule that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me bring up 1D 410149. This is a statement taken by the Office of the Prosecutor that was offered in the Martic case -- excuse me, the Milosevic case. The individual's name is Slobodan Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We will, Your Honour, just offer this for identification at this time, and we will offer this pursuant to 92 bis, after the proper certifications for 92 bis are set forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then the question arises whether it should be 92 bis or 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We will make a motion pursuant to I believe it would be 92 bis, Your Honour. Mr. Lazarevic doesn't talk specifically about any of the accused in this matter, so I think we can meet the hurdles or the qualifications of 92 ter. But be that as it may, at this point we'd just like this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, at this moment this statement Mr. Kehoe wants to put to the witness, may I take it that there is no objection against that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: As long as the proper procedure is followed, that the matter was put to the witness first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That the matter is first raised with the witness. But it might be that it has -- I do not know yet what you're going to put to the witness, Mr. Kehoe, so therefore if there is anything in the statement you want to put to the witness which has not yet been raised with him, you're invited to do so first, but it might well be that you have already extensively dealt with the matter you have put to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please first raise the issue with the witness, and if there is any need, then put Mr. Lazarevic's statement to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one additional point. I mean, for the procedure to actually have a point, it shouldn't even mention that there's a witness statement that he wants to be shown and ask for the procedure, the matter should be put forth. Otherwise, it's relatively pointless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But is done has been done. Mr. Kehoe is now invited to raise the issue with this witness before putting any statement to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Leschly, we talked about Mr. Jensen on the flow chart being in Topusko and that the Topusko office was in ARSK territory. Was Mr. Jensen collaborating with the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: That, I don't think. He spent a lot of time with them, no question about that, and talked about that, but the word "collaborate" means, you know, "do you want me to do something for you?" That, I doubt. I know -- I know he was -- he was certainly among the Danes, the one that was most pro-Serb, and he didn't hide that. I have to say that. But directly collaborate, na, I will not believe that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you know that Mr. Jensen was showing his reports to RSK officials before he sent them up to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: That, I'm not aware of, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know his interpreter? Her name is Tanja Zoric. Do you know her?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Doesn't ring a bell, no. I could have met her, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you don't recall her at all?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not Mr. Jensen was provided with a girlfriend by the RSK Intelligence Service?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you know that the RSK or the Serb Intelligence Service was working inside the ECMM to obstruct the work of the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you this statement by Mr. Lazarevic and see if it can clarify matters in any fashion. If we can turn to page 10 of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I'm looking at the clock. Perhaps -- I didn't want to interrupt you in the last series of questions, but if we start now looking at documents, I think we first should have a break. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at half past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, the Chamber has considered what we would expect you to do now, because you have the statement of Mr. Lazarevic apparently in your hands. We've got no idea what's in there, although -- well, "no idea" is too much, but what the Chamber would avoid to happen is that you put to the witness what other people might think about persons, for example, to be found in that statement, if this witness has no knowledge of the factual basis on which the other person has formed his opinion or his conclusions. So, therefore, the Chamber invites you to first focus on factual elements that may be in that statement, rather than on the conclusions, and to first verify whether those factual elements are known to this witness, whether he has -- if they are known, whether he has included -- whether he has included them in the thinking which is at the basis of his previous answers, because he was quite clear on Mr. Jensen. So, therefore, please focus on factual elements rather than on conclusions of other persons, on the basis of facts this witness might not know anything about. That should be verified first --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- as guidance for your next line of questions. Please proceed. 25

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Leschly, you told us that Mr. Jensen was very pro-Serb, and tell us a bit about why you concluded that Mr. Jensen was very pro-Serb.

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Well, he said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What did he say, exactly?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Oh, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And let me take the word "exactly" out of that. Basically, what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: I don't know. We talked a lot of words 13 years ago, and I couldn't be able to -- but he never -- he never made it a secret that he thought that the RSK was okay and should be allowed to be maintained. As well, he started in Sector East, so his first posting was out there. I mean, specific words, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But your general impression, in talking to him, was he was very much in favour of the position of the Krajina Serbs?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, I don't want to rehash old ground, but you noted for us that you didn't know Tanja Zoric, his interpreter?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: That's to say I'm certain that I met her, because when I visited him and when we met, then he would very often of course be with his interpreter, as we all did, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I mentioned to you, if you knew that the Intelligence Service for the RSK had provided Mr. Jensen with a girlfriend, and let me just take that one step further. Do you know if Mr. Jensen had a Serb girlfriend by the name of Jelena?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, during the course of Mr. Jensen being in Topusko, did you know that the RSK provided him with a house and a police guard so it looked like a miniature Danish embassy?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: No, I certainly did not. He's managed to keep that quite secret. He's a policeman, so he should know how to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How to do what?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, make sure that only what he thinks should be known outside is known outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So if Mr. Lazarevic has told the Office of the Prosecutor that Mr. Jensen would draft reports for the ECMM and show them to the RSK first to see if they agreed with them, that would be something that he would hide from you?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes, that I take it, because I hadn't heard it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, being guided by what Your Honour had to say, I do have some passages in this statement to highlight for the Chamber. I am --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's highlighting for us, then I would rather wait for the 92 bis application. We will then see what is in the statement. We will then hear from the Prosecution when they -- whether they think that it would be admissible evidence without cross-examination, and then we'll see the highlighted portions. You can highlight them then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One last issue with regard to Mr. Jensen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Jensen, after he left the Krajina and went to the ECMM office in Bosnia, do you know that he took his interpreter, Ms. Zoric, the Serb interpreter, from the Topusko office to Bosnia? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, one last issue with regard to Mr. Jensen. During the course of your conversations with Mr. Jensen, did he inform you that he had obtained the plans for Operation Storm and that he had provided the ARSK with it?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: No, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We can come back to that in one second. May I have a moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the other person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The other person that you relied upon as part of the Danish delegation was Soren Liborius; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Well, yes, but I would object to the phrase that I would rely more on compatriots than on other monitors. I would not be utterly favourable towards a fellow Dane. Yes, of course we could speak our own language, but apart from that, I hope that I dealt with all monitors in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in the course of your report, 889, in the first paragraph -- excuse me -- yeah, in the first paragraph -- before I ask you a specific question: These reports are weekly reports, assessments, and they're designed to do what, Mr. Leschly?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Well, it was something I inherited, that HRC is supposed to summarise on a weekly basis. It was something which didn't really link into the normal proceedings where you had the teams to the CCs, to the RCs, to the daily report, because the main thing that left the mission was the daily report. So I think this -- well, this was a tradition you did that, and that was handed to the headquarters, and they used it for some special report, if need be, that they might produce.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this is basically giving the headquarters a snapshot of what's happening during that week; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: M'mm-hmm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in the paragraph that you have on the first one, you complain about the Serbs using their flag and the particular currency. Do you see that on your 889? Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Well, apparently you have another numbering system than I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm talking about the Croats -- I'm talking about 889, your report of the 13th of August --

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: 889, I see nowhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, 889 is an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, P889.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we could not expect this witness to remember the exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Witness, it's your report of the 13th of August.

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Okay, yeah, that's the one called --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's it, in that paragraph. You're complaining about the flag and the currency? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Okay, yeah, yes. So what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I mean, are those yet more complaints coming from Mr. Jensen about what the Krajina Serbs are complaining about?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: No. I think this was actually, in general, something that I met right from the beginning. Now, my first stationing was in Knin, so you can imagine that's where I heard it, and I heard it from Krajina Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: That was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this is in 1995?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yeah, but this is -- this is something that came on all the time. I mean, this was -- that was normal. It's not something which is linked up with a specific meeting, specific words.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And these were issues that the Serb propaganda was complaining about, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Well, when you have a war, you have propaganda on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the Serbs, Krajina Serbs, were complaining that the Republic of Croatia was a fascist state, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Well, one of the things that struck me very much, when I arrived there, was I was told how brutal the Croats were and all the things they had done to the Serbs, and then I asked, "When was that, last week?" "No, no, no, 1941."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's speak about World War II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, unfortunately I have not yet found the passage where the flags are --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's on the 13th of August, 1995 exhibit. If you look at the summary, Your Honour, under "The Political Scene," that paragraph about midway -- about the third line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I found it, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if you can turn your attention, sir, to I believe it would be the fourth tab, which is your 27th of August, 1995 report.

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the last -- the second-to-last paragraph, and this is for the week 20 to 26th August, 1995, do you see that "travelling by train"?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Oh, yeah, that one. Yeah, I got some clobbering for that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Travelling by train through newly-conquered territory, President Tudjman delivered speeches at several stops, finally to arrive in Knin. His televised triumph tour and speeches nevertheless left the linguistic ignorant of the reminders of somebody else's arrival in Paris in 1940." That "somebody else who arrived in Paris in 1940" is Adolf Hitler, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: M'mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you, in this, are equating Franjo Tudjman with Adolf Hitler, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes, and as I said, I have been clobbered for this one, even when I was there, and I have to say apologies to very nice Croat interpreters, and I'm fully aware that this is something I shouldn't write, but still, I mean, this was a triumphant tour, it was, but probably the picture I use is not the best from somebody in a diplomatic mission. That is what you are aiming at, and that is what I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you would agree with me --

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- that when Adolf Hitler was going through Paris in 1940, he wasn't riding through land that was part of Germany, was he?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: No, no, there were a number of -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let me take a look at D741, which was Mr. Liborius' diary, page 18. This is Mr. Liborius' diary, page 18, the second paragraph, again on the 26th of August, talking about President Tudjman's liberty train tour: "Tudjman promised in his time that he would open the Zagreb-Split railway line via Knin. He was good to his word. He is cheering like the father of a country and holds a 12-minute speech with oratory results and vocal pitch, and often changes in tone of voice. His hoarseness today makes it time to remember an earlier head of state of approximately 50 years ago, not to mention any names." Now, Mr. Leschly, were you and Mr. Liborius talking about the speech given by President Tudjman and referring to him in terms of him being like Adolf Hitler?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: I honestly don't know. We -- when we met, of course, we talked a lot, but to have today to say that, yes, we specifically talked about -- absolutely sure that we make this comparison, I just wouldn't know. But it could have come up. I would not say that's impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you refer yet further about President Tudjman in your first statement, and you talk about him in paragraph 17 of your statement to the Prosecutor. Do you have that tab 1?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Paragraph 17?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Paragraph 17, the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: "It was my perception ..."?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "It was my perception that Tudjman would not support a negotiated solution."

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes, but that was -- wasn't that the military parade? Yeah, which of course should show the military strength, the capability of taking matters into military hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, had you ever met President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, were you familiar with the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes, not that I could mention any paragraph of it, but the Vance Plan as a, yes, name, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did President Tudjman negotiate for the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Was that a question or a statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the various peace plans that were presented in the former Yugoslavia, did President Tudjman negotiate through all of those plans?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the Z4 Plan?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Z4, yes, yes. I'm not familiar with it, but I know it -- it rings a bell, this "Z4."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And do you know that the Z4 plan, does this ring a bell, that part of the things to negotiate in the Z4 plan was a large degree of autonomy for the Krajina Serbs within Serbia?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Not that I -- yeah, that's probably true when you say so. I have no recollection. I have to say I didn't operate at that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, and this was -- just to clarify that yet further, I mean, the Z4 plan was a discussion about the Krajina Serbs within Croatia, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Well, don't ask me, because I don't know the -- I don't know the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: I know the existence, that there was a plan called this, but what it contains, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, just going back to your report on the 13th, you note, at the top of page 2, and that should be tab 2 in your document -- it's P889. You note massive -- there was massive ethnic cleansing. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: M'mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, what is the basis of "massive ethnic cleansing," sir?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: The basis of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, the people were gone, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How do you cleanse an -- ethnically cleanse an area when the people are gone?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Always the word "subsequent." Yeah, that's funny, yeah. I've removed "subsequent," because you're absolutely right, yes, they -- they went when things happened and not later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, this report you wrote on the 13th. That's the date of this report, and let me show you a document, 1D 530001, an ECMM document of 15 August 1995, two days after you filed your report. Now, Your Honour, I know we have raised this in writing before, but of course this is a document that was produced by the ECMM and I'd just like to repeat for the record our objection to the redactions to this document that were placed in it by the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that was -- there was a motion and it was decided, so it's already on the record, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is on the record, and you've granted our --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's not put on the record the decisions of the Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this document is Mr. Rau's report, isn't it? This is the format he used for his reports, is it not?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't -- it starts with 15/08/95, subject --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can scroll down a bit, scroll up so we see the top of the page. This is a report coming from the European Community Monitoring Mission?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yeah, they may have looked like that. That may change from presidency to presidency, how they put it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, was this the format that was being used by Mr. Rau, who we know was the head of mission in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: I honestly don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let's turn to page 3 of this document. Now, the first full paragraph, we're talking about the Serbs leaving: "Their departure seems to be final. The Krajina authorities and particularly President Martic, encouraged their citizens to leave, stressing that 'the Croats wanted the territory without its population.'" Now, looking at that quote that's in that document, and referring back to your statement where you said that the Croats wanted a land without people, can you clarify for us again whether or not you got that statement from Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: I did not. I mean, we're talking about a sentence which is hanging in the air, more or less, during those days, and who started the sentence, I haven't got a clue. You seem to have a clue, because you have these reports, but I do not recall that I've had any specific source for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the conclusion in this report is that the Krajina Serbs encouraged their citizens to leave. Now, that is contrary to the statement that you put into headquarters two days prior to that, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: It looks that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So let me set the scene, if I may, starting with your report. You are -- you are upset at this time because you believe that the Croats waited for the attention of the International Community to be focused on Srebrenica to launch Operation Storm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That mischaracterizes the witness's testimony. If he wants to refer to specific --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's fine. We'll just go straight back to the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We're talking about the second -- tab 2 in your document, your 13th report. So the second-to-last paragraph, mid paragraph: "So Croatia waited until their international friends ..." Now, who are the international friends?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Well, during my stay there it was quite obvious that the two nations that supported Croatia were Germany and the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So they waited until their international friends had helped them create "in a remarkably short time and in spite of an arms embargo, a fighting machine that could deliver the result. President Tudjman's timing was perfect. The world news had been saturated with stories of Serb atrocities in Bosnia, so it was almost amusing to follow --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for slowing down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: " ... so it was almost amusing to follow how the international media got confused, when it became clear that there was more than one Balkan army capable of unnecessary brutality. At the time when it had become quite apparent that the methods of the HV was as deplorable as those of the BSA, the US, with immaculate timing, released pictures of freshly-disturbed earth in the Srebrenica area, pushing the Croatian stories down the list of news worth covering." Now, Mr. Leschly, at this time Srebrenica had taken place, Operation Storm was over. You have a report coming from ECMM, saying that the population -- or that the President Martic encouraged the citizens to leave, and you and Mr. Liborius and others then decided to go out and do an investigation to dig up evidence of your allegations of ethnic cleansing; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: First of all, there's a mis-characterization. The report from ECMM Mr. Kehoe was referring to was on the 15th of August, so that's after the report, but just generally that's a very argumentative question. I mean, read that paragraph, ask the question about those facts, that's fine, but then to just sort of make up and argue with the witness about what is in there, I mean, if he has specific questions about the facts and what he said is one thing, but then to say, "You and Mr. Liborius made that up," that's clearly improper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I didn't say they made anything up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I didn't say they made anything up. I said that they saw this information, they -- he made an allegation of ethnic cleansing and then they went -- got together after this --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Have you got evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "You and Mr. Liborius and others then decided to go out" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which is at least ambiguous language, as to whether they decided together or not. Let's focus -- I'm aware that of course the reporting is not limited to facts. To that extent, if a witness is presented that has reported, and as he said at the beginning of his testimony, on facts and impressions, we can't exclude impressions from his testimony to further explore on what his impressions were based. At the same time, I agree with Mr. Hedaraly that even admitting that it's not just about facts, that we should put certain limits to how argumentative the questions should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, at this time I'll offer into evidence 1D 530001, the ECMM report of 15 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D798.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D798 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to D741, page 13, again back to the diary of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will appear on your screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Liborius.

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The top of the page. Now, the report I just read to you was the 15th. The 16 of August: "Today, first contact with UMN." What is that?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: That's the Danish Administrative Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "What in the world is going on with the Spanish presidency." Now, Javier Solana was the ECMM president at the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I believe that the head of mission in Zagreb, Mr. Sanchez Rau, was Spanish as well.

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes:

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Mette and I are quickly coming to agree that I sent her 36 pages of documents that differentiate the picture." Now, Mette is Mette Neilsen; right?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
