utterances.text: And Mette Neilsen is from the Danish Foreign Ministry?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: She's the one I reported to, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And Mette Neilsen right now is the Danish ambassador to Serbia, isn't she?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: That, I don't know. I haven't followed these people for many, many years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, when was the last time you spoke to Mr. Liborius?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Oh, all the way back to when I left September 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The next paragraph: "Now I have a sense that I am away from Knin, away from the center of events in this part of Croatia. I discussed this situation with HRC ..." That's you, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "And suggest I go quickly to Knin and again to put some of the emphasis there." So, Mr. Leschly, you had a discussion with Mr. Liborius, after this ECMM report came out, that Martic encouraged the citizens to leave, and did you tell him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: He can finish the question. I just want to object.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you tell him that he should go out and develop evidence of ethnic cleansing in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I mean, first of all, I think that he has to ask the foundation to the witness if he remembers that meeting. Just showing him someone else's diary of a meeting is not a foundation for that meeting. And we should actually do the same thing with someone else's statement. Ask him independently if he remembers such a meeting before putting something to suggest to the witness what occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there is a clear reference to it, to a meeting, I don't consider it inadmissible to put it to the witness, and I expect you, that if a question is asked about a meeting where you would come to the conclusion that you don't remember that meeting, that you would tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I do not impose on the parties the duty that if such a clear clue is already in evidence, that it should be verified. It may also depend on what witness is in front of us. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you have a discussion with Mr. Liborius to go out and put together a report concerning the consequences in the RSK of Operation Storm to support your allegations of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: No, I don't have a recollection of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you have a recollection of having a conversation with Mr. Liborius after you received this report that we showed you from the 15th of August?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: No. I have -- we -- I don't know. If he was in Zagreb then, we would talk to each other many, many times during the day, and if he was elsewhere, we might be on the phone. We did not conduct meetings. It was as one monitor to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, it was a little more than one monitor to the other. You were the head of the Danish delegation, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And Soren Liborius --

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Took over after me and was employed by the foreign ministry, had a very -- well, he was very well respected, much more than I. I was just a normal, old reserve officer, taking care of the delegation. He was the sharp brain that would write the sharp reports, and our role was very much like that and in respect of each other's capabilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So because he was the one who would write the sharp reports, did you tell him to go out and write a report about consequences in Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did he -- let me show you P815. This is a report by Mr. Liborius of the 26th of August, where he has the initial consequences in former RSK of Operation Storm. Do you remember this report, sir?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: I'm sure I've seen it, yes, but I don't -- if you ask me to tell you what's in it, I wouldn't be able to do that in any detail, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So if we went through the contents of this report, you wouldn't have any recollection of this report?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Some of it, I may recognise when I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go through some of it, then. Go to four pages in. One more page, please. Now, let's just look at this report, and in this report is a list of villages. As you can see at the top, it notes burning and destruction, observations of burning and destruction by ECMM operating in the southern part of Sector South. Do you remember reviewing this list of villages being destroyed?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Specifically, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You have no knowledge of that. Okay. Now, just looking at this as an ECMM head of the Regional Centre and looking at the timing of this, being the 26th of August, let me just look, for instance, at the Gradac document. Do you see that, right below -- towards the bottom of the page? Just scroll back down before that. It says: "Visit on 1245, houses being set on fire, deserted." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: M'mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you looked at that, sir, would you assume that that was a Serb village that -- without any further explanation, that that was a Serb village that was being set on fire?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yeah, that particular time, yes, I would probably, because the date says "9th of August, 1995."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, during this period of time, did anybody ever explain -- or you don't recall this report, so I would take it that you don't know that, for instance, in the 1991 census, that Gradac had a 96 per cent population of Croats. Now, as a head of the regional office, HRC, would you expect that type of detail to be set forth in a report like this so that you, as his superior, would completely understand the full nature of the damage in Sector South and who it was done by?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Well, when you look at -- I don't know. Perhaps I should have the -- let's see the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is rather complex.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. It's not a "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me rephrase it for you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This village, Gradac -- and there are pages of them. This village, Gradac, it's on the first page, had a census -- in the 1991 census, that was a Croat village, 96 per cent?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you read this, you told us you would have concluded that this was a Serb village being burnt?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yeah, well, I -- actually, Gradac was one of the first areas I actually went to as a monitor in the field, and it was very noticeable that there were a lot of burned-out houses and they had burned out four years before -- no, two years before. We're now talking 1993. But in August 1995, if a house is burning, it's probably not a Croatian house in Gradac, because, as you said yesterday, it was mainly Croatian or Croat, but there were some Serbs as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So based on your answer, you would have concluded that the Croats were burning their own houses?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: No, that's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go into this meeting with General Gotovina if we can, and I think that that's if we can. That should be your tab 6, sir.

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that is P893, for the record. Now, in this report --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On the first page of the report, you were talking about having a meeting with the Zupan, and I'm talking about the bottom of that. And you note in this report that Croatia's reputation as -- "The damage to Croatia's reputation is experienced because of the ethnic cleansing measures undertaken by Croatians, with or without consent from official authorities. Zupan was very forthright in his regret that not more had been done to establish law and order through a state of emergency in the newly-liberated areas and maybe even martial law." Now, the Zupan was telling you that they made a mistake not declaring a state of emergency or declaring martial law, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Now, 13 years after that meeting, and with this text, all I can say, that apparently it was his regret. I'm not saying that he would -- what was the word you used -- that they had made a mistake. That, I mean, I don't know what -- what the word was, but apparently I've written "his regret," and that's not the same as saying it's a major mistake. He felt a little bit sorry, that's probably the way he said it, since I had written it like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That he regretted it didn't happen?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, martial law states that the army takes over the area; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: I believe that varies from country to country. I don't know. I'm not a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You do know that as of the 6th of August of 1995, the civilian institutions took over at least in Sector South, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Could be. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, did you -- when you took over your position in September of 1995 as the head of the Regional Centre in Zagreb, did you learn that, when the Republic of Croatia took over the -- when the civilian authorities took over in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Now I'm utterly confused. I took over -- I took over on the 6th of July. That's one thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you took over the Regional Centre Zagreb under the reorganisation plan and Sector South came under your control or your chain of command --

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Okay, yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- did you learn at that time that the Republic of Croatia constitutional order and civilian authorities took over on the 6th of August?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: I probably have been told.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But you don't recall at this time?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn your attention in this report to your conversation with General Gotovina, if we can. I'm just getting this number correct. Now, you write: "Lieutenant General Gotovina was asked if he shared the Zadar Zupan's opinion that the need for the state of emergency in order to have avoided the killings, lootings, and burnings, his only remark, only remark, was, 'What killings,' after which he went into an attack on the International Community that had no moral right to moral slapping of Croatia." Now, let us turn our attention to P895, which is the report of the 20th September, 1995. Now, in this report, Mr. Leschly, in paragraph 2, it notes that a number of issues were discussed, among them the possibility of ECMM to patrol at the Bosnian side of the border: "So far it is not possible, and the general promised to inform us when. "Asked about the ongoing looting, arson and harassment, the general's opinion is that the police have to control the situation ..." Did General Gotovina, in your conversation on the 20th of September, tell you that the police have to control the situation?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: According to Stig Marker-Hansen, he did, and if you ask me now if I remember it, no, I didn't, because I don't remember individual sentences from a meeting 13 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, do you have any reason to question that Stig Marker-Hansen wrote down that he said that the police have to control the situation?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: No, I mean that's -- that's quite likely, oh, absolutely, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You would agree with me, then, that that is not in your report?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: That is true, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So when you wrote in your report, back on the 24th of September, 1995, that this was General Gotovina's only remark, that wasn't accurate, was it?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: It looked that way -- looks that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In fact, it's not the whole truth as to what happened during the course of that meeting, was it?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: No, apparently not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He next said that: "Croatia is still a nation with a constitution and law and order. Any person committing crimes will be charged." Now, he said that too, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Excuse me -- yes, oh, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I think you will agree with me that that is not in the report as well.

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: M'mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hansen writes in the report that: "A war is always followed by disasters, and now things are under control. The general has no objection for Serbs to live in Croatia." Did he tell you that, too?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Probably. I mean, during a meeting of 45 minutes, and you're down to lines, you can't expect every single sentence to go in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I understand, sir, but you had this meeting on the 20th of September, 1995. You wrote a report on the 24th of September, 1995, where you note that the only thing that General Gotovina said was expressing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you have done this now several times. In the statement of the witness, he said his only remark was in response to what apparently the witness raised, and then he continues that: " ... after which he went into ..." And then apparently refers to many, many words Mr. Gotovina would have spoken at that time. So to say -- you to say the only words he spoke was, that appears to be not a proper reflection of what the evidence of this witness is. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, suffice it to say, without going into this, your report concerning what General Gotovina said concerning controlling -- area being controlled by the police, that Croatia being a country of law and order, and that crimes -- people committing crimes were being charged, were not included in your report?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness has given these answers already, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do see that you want to emphasise certain matters, but let's not put the same questions where the answers are crystal clear that it was not part of his report. And from your questions, it's perfectly clear to the Chamber as well that these are important issues for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say "well, suffice it to say." May it suffice that the Chamber is well aware, without being told two or three times, what you find of importance. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Obviously this is a very important issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And we have this opportunity under the Rules to put this to the witness, and this is our opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but under my guidance you have not the opportunity to put it two or three times to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would you please -- I'm concerned about your last response, that what right you have under the Rules, where a minute before I told you that our guidance was that you should not repeat questions just to emphasise matters, because nowhere in the Rules it says that you can seek repetitious evidence in order to emphasise your point of view. Would you please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn our attention to 65 ter 4254.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This, Mr. Leschly, is an ECMM daily monitoring activity report. Are you familiar with this format, sir?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 2, the second-to-last paragraph from the bottom on page 2. I'm sorry, I think I might have the wrong document here, Your Honour. I might have pulled up the wrong document. It should be 65 ter 2448. My apologies. I read the wrong number. My apologies, Mr. Leschly.

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Well, it's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a daily monitoring report of 21 September for activities of 20 December, and going to the second page -- I misspoke. It's the -- it is a report of the 21st of September for activities of the 20th of September. The second page, again in the second-to-last paragraph, denotes the conversation with General Gotovina, the commander of the operation zone of Split: "General Gotovina said to ECMM that burning, looting and harassment must be stopped by the police, but added that he regards 'hatred towards an enemy who has burned, looted and expelled one's family as a normal human reaction.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we'll offer into evidence 65 ter 2448.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Was there a question being put to the witness about this report? I have no objection. Just wondering.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'll ask the witness after I offer -- ask the question after I offer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be no objection. Although the usual way is to first put questions, it's not a major problem. Mr. Registrar, that would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number D799, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Exhibit D799 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Leschly, these reports that we have discussed written by Stig Marker-Hansen say nothing about any questions about killings or doubt about killings that were -- that you say were raised by General Gotovina. Do you have any explanation for that, sir?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: None other than every report cannot cover everything. No, I have no explanation why.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General Gotovina's comment in the report about hatred towards an enemy who burned and looted and expelled, you understood him to mean that there was an element of revenge coming from people who had been persecuted by the Krajina Serbs; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Well, this is not something that I wrote. This is something that Mr. Hansen wrote. And, yes, the way it's presented here, yes, the word that pops up in one's brain is the word "revenge," and I think that's a fair comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And whether or not it is wrong or right, you understood the "revenge" element that was taking place in the Krajina, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, we mentioned that there was nothing in either Stig Marker-Hansen's report or the ECMM headquarters report of the 21st of September about killings. Could it be, sir, that this was simply a conversation with General Gotovina about burning, looting and harassment?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: I -- it's -- I mean, when it's put down a few days after what had happened, then I would imagine that it must have been said, because I don't think I would -- I would never sit down and write something which I know is deliberately wrong. But we also have, of course, to -- hopefully, that the interpreters are doing their job so that we don't get even the small tilting of words.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You say that, sir, but you know what you wrote down in your --

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Oh, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- report is not the whole truth; right?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you -- oh, there was no verbal -- you were nodding your head "yes" to that?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes, okay, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let me turn your attention to -- not only from your report, but you note in the last item of P893, which is the 20th of September -- excuse me, the 24th of September document: "New nations are naturally very nationalistic in the early stages, and as he put it, 'Once Sector East is home,' he would possibly become more liberal, but not for now." Let us turn attention to paragraph 44 of your statement, starting in the second sentence: "In the context of our conversation, I understood that the statement of General Gotovina referring to Sector East, to mean that once Sector East was captured, he would be more of a peacetime commander and less strict in his conduct against the Serbian population."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Community."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, "Serbian community." Thank you, Your Honour. "This was to be an indirect admission that the looting and destruction of Serbian property was allowed to go on."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, given that General Gotovina told you that the police have to control the situation, that Croatia is a nation of law and order, and that criminals will be charged, on what basis did you conclude that he made an indirect admission that the looting and destruction of Serbian property was allowed to go on? What fact did you learn of that allowed you to conclude that?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Well, first of all, when you mention the things that were said about the Croatian policies, one of the main problems in this time was the discrepancy between what the official Croatia said that they wanted to do and what happened in the field, because there was a huge difference. And you've had all these administrative harassments, which are also mentioned elsewhere, so when you've -- let's see, it's 44. Sector East then came up, as I mentioned earlier today. Sector East was very much on everybody's mind at the time, because that was the remaining part not under Croatian control, and when General Gotovina then said that -- that once that is under Croatian control, he might be less strict, he probably has felt that while it was still there, there was a kind of state of war or a state of not at least peace, because things haven't finished, and therefore he had to be strict. And when I then say that the looting and destruction of property was allowed to go on, the fact of the matter was, in the field, that, yes, they did go on at that time, regardless of what the official Croatia claimed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Leschly, was this -- was this some silent admission by General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Well, that was the way apparently I interpreted it at the time. That's all I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you interpreted it as a silent admission?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes, I have done that, from what I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you talk to Mr. Liborius about this silent admission?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that your comment about this silent admission by General Gotovina that looting and destruction of Serbian property was allowed to go on, is in direct contradiction to Stig Marker-Hansen's report reflecting the conversation with General Gotovina that criminals will be prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes, it is, but there is a discrepancy between what was being said during these months and what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you, based on what he said, concluded that he made an admission about allowing looting and burning to go on in the same conversation where he told you that criminals would be prosecuted; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, that's now again -- I thought I had been clear enough on repetition, and the matter has been dealt with sufficiently. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions. Mr. Leschly, thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Other Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Nothing arises. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, is there any need to put further questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Leschly, before the reorganisation in late August of ECMM, did you receive the reports by RC Knin to the ECMM headquarters?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Not automatically. They came separate. If I wanted to see it, I could see it. And I can't remember whether it was c.c.'ed. Maybe it was. Did we send them to the others as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Could we have P830, please, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we didn't send it sideways.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: On the screen in front of you is a report from the 10th of August from -- the contents of it are not to my interest. I just want to see the top part, the send line. So it's from RC Knin to the ECMM headquarter; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And then you see in the info, it goes to RC Zagreb is included?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: It is, yes. Okay, so we were c.c.'ed. Yes, I couldn't remember whether -- I think in certain periods, we did, and in certain periods, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And when you would prepare your -- when you would prepare your weekly reports, you would review all the reports that you had received in the preceding week?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Yes. Mostly, of course, our own, but, yes, a Knin report would also be there but not -- normally not Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kehoe asked you several times, apparently in a formulation that he likes very much, whether your --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, please, please, I object to the comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Come on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're right. Mr. Hedaraly, would you please refrain from commenting. Even without your objection, I might have intervened, Mr. Hedaraly. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Leschly, Mr. Kehoe asked you several times about whether your report was the whole truth. Now, Mr. Leschly, did you ever write anything in your report that you knew was false?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: No, I never did that. I may have -- as I -- if I'd been in doubt, I would have left it out, in anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So when you said that it may not have been the whole truth, what did you mean?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Well, it meant that, of course, during a meeting lasting one hour, and you had to sum up, you can only take this and take that, and there will be a lot which hasn't been covered. That's the nature of report-writing. Of course, you can hope that you take out the more important parts, but that is up to one's own discretion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Leschly. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Leschly, one question, which is the following:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You used the word, I think - let me just find it - looting, arson and killings. You've seen it in documents, "looting, arson and harassment" has been used. Looking at these reports, does there come any doubt in your mind as to whether you raised the issue of arson, looting and killing? Because earlier it was said that you never know with translators, but in your statement we read that you asked him whether he shared Zadar Zupan's opinion about the need for a state of emergency in order to have avoided the killings, lootings and burnings. Even if it would have been translated wrongly to you in your conversation, are you -- having seen this, comes there a doubt to your mind as to whether you mentioned "killings" in this when you put it to Mr. Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: I have no way today to even substantiate at that time, but if I wrote it, what was it, three or four days after, it must have been said. That would be what I -- what I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to put this in order to be -- that there could be no ambiguity in this respect. Have the questions by Mr. Hedaraly or by the Bench, have they triggered any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I have more clarification on your question, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Leschly, this is on page 17 of -- page 17, line 14 -- 15, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Today's transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Today's transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Leschly, you are not able to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- manipulate it. We'll have a look at it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So there is no question about it, this is what you just testified to previously this afternoon: "So there is no question about it that when it was mentioned about why do these things take place, I must have thought at the time that General Gotovina did not recognise killings or lootings or burnings. I think that what 'killings' covers, these activities overall." So in response to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It was "these atrocities" on the one he said, and it's a draft transcript, but that's what the witness had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It says "activities."

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It says "activities."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, how is this triggered by my question or by Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: By your question, Judge, because with regard to these killings, what he's talking about there and what he said in the transcript was that that encompassed not just killings, and your question was isolated to just killings, when the witness, in his testimony, is talking about virtually all crimes are encompassed in that comment that he made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, put the question to the witness, if you want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you put that in your comment about what killings, you were talking about General Gotovina raising a question about what crime, "What crimes are you talking about"; isn't that what you meant to say?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: Well, as I say, to the best of my knowledge, if I wrote down that he had used the word "those killings," I would have -- I would think that that was being used. But what it covers, I think that -- I think that doesn't mean that he has admitted to the other -- this is what I'm saying. I'm sure that it covered everything, what -- always, "What are you talking about?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, "What are you talking about" with regard to crime; right? Isn't that what you're saying, sir?

utterances.speaker: LENNART LESCHLY
utterances.text: No. I'm saying that this answer that he I'm quite sure has given, otherwise, I wouldn't have written it, I'm sure that that would take care of the other words that we're talking about here in rejecting, in rejecting the conduct of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a conversation that is taking place at the same time that he is saying that criminals should be prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you're really restarting your examination. That's not -- you said you would seek a clarification. You have sufficiently done that, and you could have done that at an earlier stage, by the way, because Mr. Hedaraly, exactly on those same lines, said that he had a language issue, whether he fully understood, and then you objected against that question put to the witness. So, therefore, I think that the clarification -- the question about the clarification has been put to the witness and the witness has answered those questions. Any other questions triggered by the questions by the Bench? This means, Mr. Leschly, that this concludes your evidence in this court. Of course, we're happy that you could travel back after you had given your evidence rather than to travel back and then have to return. I'd like to thank you for coming to The Hague, for having answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe trip home again. We adjourn, and we will resume on Monday, the 22nd of September, quarter past 2.00, in Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 22nd day of September, 2008, at 2.15 p.m. 25
